entries.title: Loschmidt’s Reversibility Objection
entries.scope: Claim-level source audit of the complete assigned article: setup and dynamical assumptions for velocity reversal; entropy interpretation and inference; Boltzmann’s immediate reply versus his later statistical account; low-entropy-past explanations; the H-theorem and qualifications; historical chronology; distinction between Loschmidt’s reversibility objection and the Poincaré/Zermelo recurrence argument; and editorial teaching framing. The matching dataset object and expansion-record entry were checked for alignment. No expert review is claimed.
entries.summary: The article’s treatment of exact reversal, Boltzmann and Gibbs entropy, statistical typicality, Boltzmann’s separate 1877 arguments, low-entropy boundary conditions, the H-theorem assumption, and the Zermelo distinction is traceable to relevant passages. The independent review directly read p. 139 of the original Loschmidt scan; the article and ledger now state this limited access accurately. Dataset and article Further Reading URLs match.

sources.title: Thermodynamic Asymmetry in Time
sources.author: Craig Callender
sources.publication: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; first published 2001, current online entry consulted
sources.access_level: Relevant full-text sections and passages retrieved and read (including the discussion of the H-theorem, Loschmidt and Zermelo objections, and §3.1, ‘Past Hypothesis’); not every section of the entry was reviewed.
sources.exact_locations_read: Discussion beginning ‘Trouble looms over this explanation of time asymmetry’ in §3, including the paragraphs contrasting Loschmidt’s time-reversal objection with Zermelo’s recurrence objection; §3.1 ‘Past Hypothesis’, including Boltzmann’s fluctuation proposal and the modern naming attributed to Albert (2000). The entry also quotes Loschmidt (1876, p. 139).
sources.limitations: Secondary reference, not an original paper. The passage explains the objections at an overview level and does not supply a full derivation of the phase-space or kinetic assumptions. Its current copy includes material beyond the historical dates of the initial entry publication.

sources.title: Boltzmann’s Work in Statistical Physics
sources.author: Jos Uffink
sources.publication: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, archived Summer 2013 edition; first published 2004
sources.source_type: Scholarly reference work / secondary historical and philosophical analysis
sources.access_level: Relevant full-text sections retrieved and read: selected passages in §§1.2, 3.2–3.3, 4, and 5.2; not the entire article for unrelated topics.
sources.exact_locations_read: §1.2 distinguishes the reversibility objection (Loschmidt) from the recurrence objection (Zermelo) and dates Zermelo’s challenge to 1896; §3.2 discusses the assumptions and status of Boltzmann’s H-theorem, including the Stoßzahlansatz; §3.3 quotes Loschmidt (1876, p. 139), states the modern Hamiltonian time-reversal formulation, and discusses Boltzmann’s immediate 1877 response and its limitations; §4 treats the 1877b permutational argument; §5.2 includes Boltzmann’s 1895 formulation of the statistical H-theorem and further debate.
sources.limitations: A scholarly interpretation, not primary text. Uffink explicitly notes disagreement among historians/commentators about the content and status of Boltzmann’s early H-theorem and response; those disputes are reported rather than resolved by this audit.

sources.title: Boltzmann’s Reply to the Loschmidt Paradox: A Commented Translation
sources.author: Olivier Darrigol
sources.publication: The European Physical Journal H, vol. 46, article 29 (2021), https://doi.org/10.1140/epjh/s13129-021-00029-2; the author’s openly accessible HAL item is an early draft and expressly directs readers to cite the published version
sources.source_type: Peer-reviewed historical secondary analysis with translated primary passages; consulted full text was the author’s prepublication draft
sources.access_level: Relevant full-text passages read in the accessible early draft at https://hal.science/hal-03467467/document; the published Springer page was also inspected but exposed only its abstract, notes, and limited preview material rather than the full article.
sources.exact_locations_read: Early draft §1 ‘The Loschmidt paradox’ (translation of Loschmidt 1876 and historical context; especially the discussion of reversing all atomic velocities and the original example); §2 translation of Boltzmann’s 1877a response (Wiener Berichte, pp. 116–122; especially the construction of opposite initial conditions and reversal of the sign of the thermodynamic integral); §§3–4 commentary and clarified account of Boltzmann’s probability argument; §5 discussion of later qualifications. The draft’s opening states that it is an early version and says to cite the published EPJH article.
sources.limitations: The full text directly read is a prepublication draft, not the final published version. The final version’s full text was not accessible through the inspected Springer page. The translated primary passages are mediated by Darrigol; modern terms such as microstate and macrostate are explicitly the commentator’s explanatory vocabulary.

sources.title: Poincare Recurrence Theorem (1890–1897)
sources.author: University of Maryland, Mathematics History page; individual author not stated on page
sources.publication: University of Maryland Department of Mathematics history resource; updated 24 August 2001
sources.access_level: Full short webpage read.
sources.exact_locations_read: Opening two paragraphs: identifies Poincaré’s recurrence theorem (1890), describes recurrence for bounded fixed-energy mechanical systems, and states that Zermelo used it in 1896 as a separate objection to the Second Law; final paragraph summarizes Boltzmann’s statistical response to recurrences.
sources.limitations: Concise university-hosted explainer, not Poincaré’s or Zermelo’s original text and not a detailed mathematical proof. The distinction is also supported by Callender and Uffink.

sources.title: Translation of Ludwig Boltzmann’s Paper ‘On the Relationship between the Second Fundamental Theorem of the Mechanical Theory of Heat and Probability Calculations Regarding the Conditions for Thermal Equilibrium’
sources.author: Ludwig Boltzmann; translated and commented by Kim Sharp and Franz Matschinsky
sources.publication: Entropy 17(4) (2015), pp. 1971–2009; English translation of Boltzmann’s 1877b paper, DOI 10.3390/e17041971
sources.source_type: Primary text in modern English translation, with editorial scientific commentary
sources.access_level: Full HTML article was available; the relevant translated text in §V was read.
sources.exact_locations_read: Section V, ‘Relationship of the Entropy to That Quantity Which I Have Called the Probability Distribution’, including the discussion of multiplicity/‘permutability’ and the relationship of that measure to entropy (exact section heading in the HTML; journal page range not independently verified).
sources.limitations: This is Boltzmann’s separate 1877b combinatorial/statistical paper, not the immediate 1877a reply to Loschmidt. Translation and commentary are modern; the text’s terminology does not map one-to-one onto all contemporary probability interpretations.

sources.title: Über den Zustand des Wärmegleichgewichtes eines Systems von Körpern mit Rücksicht auf die Schwerkraft. I
sources.author: Josef (Joseph) Loschmidt
sources.publication: Wiener Berichte 73 (1876), pp. 128–142; source scan hosted by the Loschmidt Laboratory biography site
sources.access_level: Original scan opened and p. 139 directly read during independent follow-up; the complete paper was not read.
sources.exact_locations_read: Page 139, describing reversal of all atomic velocities and the retrograde course of events; corroborated with Darrigol’s translation and the SEP quotation.
sources.limitations: Only p. 139 was read directly from the original scan. Other relevant historical passages were checked through Darrigol’s accessible early draft and scholarly reference works.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The exact-reversal construction requires fixed positions and simultaneous reversal of all relevant velocities/momenta, under time-reversal-invariant mechanical equations; it then retraces the prior trajectory.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §3.3, paragraphs beginning ‘Putting the point in more modern terms’; this states the Hamiltonian time-reversal transformation as reversing velocities and replacing t by −t. See also the embedded Loschmidt quotation at p. 139.
claim_evidence.finding: The source explicitly supports the trajectory-reversal claim and frames the objection as applying to Hamiltonian mechanics. Darrigol’s translated Loschmidt passage likewise says to reverse all atomic velocities and explains the resulting reversed course.
claim_evidence.limitation: The exact-reversal statement presumes a mechanically isolated/full relevant system and a time-reversal-invariant interaction law; the idealization is not a practical procedure for an ordinary gas.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Article now states the all-velocity reversal, fixed positions, time-reversal-invariant dynamics, complete relevant system, and exact-retracing conditions.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The gas-spreading-from-a-corner scenario is an explanatory teaching variation rather than the literal setup in Loschmidt’s 1876 passage.
claim_evidence.source_title: Boltzmann’s Reply to the Loschmidt Paradox: A Commented Translation
claim_evidence.exact_location: Darrigol accessible early draft, §1 ‘The Loschmidt paradox’, especially its account of Loschmidt’s one-molecule/device example and translation of Loschmidt (1876, p. 139); the draft also notes that Loschmidt’s article’s primary concern was the gas-column temperature argument.
claim_evidence.finding: Loschmidt’s own example concerns a specially prepared state with one molecule carrying energy and the others initially at rest, evolving to a stationary state before all velocities are reversed. The article’s corner-gas image captures the general reversible construction but is not his exact case.
claim_evidence.limitation: The original scan itself was not readable; the historical comparison is based on Darrigol’s translation/commentary and Uffink’s quotation.
claim_evidence.required_edit: The revised article explicitly labels the corner-gas description a modern teaching illustration and summarizes the different historical example.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The reversed trajectory exhibits a decrease of entropy as the gas returns to its earlier macrostate.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §3 discussion of the H-theorem and Loschmidt objection: time reversal gives a mirror entropy-decreasing solution for each entropy-increasing solution; compare the quoted Loschmidt passage at p. 139 in Uffink §3.3.
claim_evidence.finding: The claim is supported when ‘entropy’ means the thermodynamic/Boltzmann macrostate quantity used in the argument. It should not be read as a decrease of the fine-grained Gibbs entropy under ideal Hamiltonian flow.
claim_evidence.limitation: The cited SEP passage is schematic and does not elaborate the distinctions among entropy definitions; the fine-grained Gibbs-entropy qualification follows from the Hamiltonian setting, not from the historical wording of Loschmidt’s paper.
claim_evidence.required_edit: The article now specifies Boltzmann macro-entropy and distinguishes it from fine-grained Gibbs entropy.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Loschmidt’s objection implies that reversible mechanics cannot entail a universal, exceptionless monotonic entropy increase for every mechanically allowed microstate.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §3, passage stating it is impossible to get a function of the classical state to monotonically increase from conservative dynamics alone and that Loschmidt’s time-reversal objection yields a mirror entropy-decreasing solution.
claim_evidence.finding: The objection blocks an unrestricted universal monotonicity theorem from reversible dynamics alone; it does not show that observed macroscopic entropy decreases are common or that statistical mechanics is false.
claim_evidence.limitation: The inference targets a proposed universal derivation, not every qualified statistical, kinetic, or coarse-grained account of the second law.
claim_evidence.required_edit: The article narrows its conclusion to the impossibility of deriving monotonic increase on every allowed trajectory from reversible mechanics alone.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Boltzmann’s immediate 1877 reply treated exceptional H-increasing/reversed states as extremely improbable, but this reply is distinct from the later 1877b permutational argument and its adequacy is debated.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §3.3, ‘Boltzmann’s response (1877a)’: exceptional states, improbability, and critique of the reversal-invariant probability assignment; §4, ‘1877b: The permutational argument’, on the later macrostate/multiplicity argument.
claim_evidence.finding: The source explicitly separates Boltzmann’s immediate response from the later 1877b probability treatment and questions whether the former resolves the objection. Darrigol’s translated/commented 1877a text supplies the underlying passage and discusses its assumptions.
claim_evidence.limitation: Historians disagree over the meaning, assumptions, and success of Boltzmann’s response; the article appropriately reports it as a reply, not a settled solution.
claim_evidence.required_edit: The article now separates the 1877a reply from the 1877b multiplicity argument and states that interpretive/adequacy questions remain debated.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Boltzmann’s later statistical explanation treats equilibrium as having far greater multiplicity/phase-space volume than non-equilibrium macrostates, making entropy increase typical under probability assumptions rather than necessary for every microstate.
claim_evidence.source_title: Translation of Ludwig Boltzmann’s Paper ‘On the Relationship between the Second Fundamental Theorem…’
claim_evidence.exact_location: §V, ‘Relationship of the Entropy to That Quantity Which I Have Called the Probability Distribution’; read with Uffink, SEP ‘Boltzmann’s Work in Statistical Physics’, §4, on the 1877b permutational argument and macrostate multiplicity.
claim_evidence.finding: The translated primary text connects the equilibrium distribution’s permutability measure with entropy; Uffink explains this in modern macrostate/phase-space terms. This supports a typicality/statistical account but does not alone justify treating probability as an unconditional dynamical tendency.
claim_evidence.limitation: The Sharp–Matschinsky text is Boltzmann’s separate 1877b paper, not his immediate 1877a reply; Boltzmann’s historical probability concepts and modern probability measures are not interchangeable without qualification.
claim_evidence.required_edit: The article now describes the later argument separately and qualifies probability as dependent on specified assumptions.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The apparent statistical direction problem remains: a time-symmetric distribution over states at a non-equilibrium macrostate can make higher-entropy antecedents typical as well as higher-entropy successors.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §3 paragraphs following the reversibility objection, beginning ‘An objection in their spirit (specifically, Loschmidt’s) can also be advanced against Boltzmann’s later view’; paired statements (1) and (2) for typical future and past macrostates.
claim_evidence.finding: The source directly states the time-symmetric statistical dilemma. This is why the entropy-multiplicity reply does not, by itself, explain why the observed arrow points toward the future.
claim_evidence.limitation: This is a philosophical/statistical formulation; detailed resolution depends on a chosen measure, conditioning information, and cosmological boundary assumptions.
claim_evidence.required_edit: The article now notes that the statistical account alone does not select a temporal direction.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The modern Past Hypothesis is a low-entropy-past boundary condition used with statistical mechanics; it is conceptually distinct from Loschmidt’s objection and from Boltzmann’s entire 1877 reply, while Boltzmann’s fluctuation cosmology is a related but different proposal.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §3.1 ‘Past Hypothesis’, including the paragraph naming Albert (2000), the statement that Boltzmann explained the observable universe as a fluctuation in a larger universe, and the discussion of the low-entropy past boundary condition.
claim_evidence.finding: The source directly supports the low-entropy-past distinction and identifies Boltzmann’s fluctuation account separately from the contemporary Past Hypothesis terminology.
claim_evidence.limitation: The Past Hypothesis is a current philosophical framing, not a label used by Loschmidt in 1876 or necessarily a complete description of Boltzmann’s evolving views.
claim_evidence.required_edit: The article now separates the modern boundary-condition approach from the historical objection and notes Boltzmann’s distinct fluctuation proposal.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The Boltzmann H-theorem is not a conclusion of reversible mechanics without kinetic assumptions; the Stoßzahlansatz/molecular-chaos assumption contributes time asymmetry.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §3.2, discussion of the special assumptions in the H-theorem and the Stoßzahlansatz; §3.3, final paragraph on Burbury (1894a) and Bryan (1894) identifying its time-asymmetric role.
claim_evidence.finding: The source supports the article’s qualification that the H-theorem has assumptions beyond reversible microscopic mechanics. It presents the interpretation and historical identification of the Stoßzahlansatz as part of scholarly analysis, not as an uncontroversial exhaustive list of every assumption.
claim_evidence.limitation: This audit did not reproduce the kinetic derivation; ‘molecular chaos’ is a common explanatory label but does not mean random behavior in an unrestricted everyday sense.
claim_evidence.required_edit: The article now names the Stoßzahlansatz/molecular-chaos assumption and denies that the H-theorem follows from reversible mechanics alone.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The Poincaré recurrence theorem and Zermelo’s 1896 recurrence objection are distinct from Loschmidt’s velocity-reversal objection.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Opening two paragraphs, which identify Poincaré’s theorem (1890), state its recurrence consequence for bounded fixed-energy systems, and describe Zermelo’s use of it in 1896; cross-check Uffink §1.2 and Callender §3 for the separate Loschmidt/reversibility versus Zermelo/recurrence labels.
claim_evidence.finding: The distinction and chronology are supported: Poincaré’s mathematical recurrence result is not itself Loschmidt’s reversal construction; Zermelo made a separate 1896 objection based on recurrence.
claim_evidence.limitation: The Maryland page is a concise educational account, not the primary mathematical publication or Zermelo’s paper. The article does not assert detailed theorem conditions beyond bounded mechanical systems.
claim_evidence.required_edit: The article now explicitly separates recurrence from velocity reversal and identifies Zermelo’s 1896 objection as distinct.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Loschmidt’s objection is historically associated with a 1876 publication and Boltzmann’s immediate response with 1877; Boltzmann’s probability/multiplicity paper is a separate 1877 work.
claim_evidence.source_title: Boltzmann’s Reply to the Loschmidt Paradox: A Commented Translation
claim_evidence.exact_location: Darrigol early draft §1 and §2; footnote 1 identifies Loschmidt 1876 and Boltzmann 1877a, pp. 116–122. Uffink, SEP, §§3.3–4, distinguishes 1877a response from 1877b permutational argument; Callender’s SEP bibliography identifies Loschmidt 1876/1877 and Zermelo 1896.
claim_evidence.finding: The article’s formerly approximate ‘1870s’ dating was safe but uninformative. The revised chronology is precise about the core publication and reply while avoiding a claim that this was the first-ever anticipation of the general idea.
claim_evidence.limitation: William Thomson anticipated aspects of the paradox earlier (Darrigol note 4); the article focuses on Loschmidt’s historically named objection, not priority for every related insight.
claim_evidence.required_edit: The article now identifies Loschmidt’s 1876 publication and Boltzmann’s 1877 immediate reply, and lists Zermelo’s 1896 objection separately.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The claims that velocity reversal of every molecule is practically infeasible and that the objection does not demonstrate routine entropy decreases are properly qualified as a practical point, not as a rebuttal to its mathematical possibility.
claim_evidence.source_title: Boltzmann’s Reply to the Loschmidt Paradox: A Commented Translation
claim_evidence.exact_location: Darrigol early draft §1 commentary after the translated Loschmidt passage (the reversal is a conceivable but not practically feasible undoing of history); footnote 6 notes concrete Loschmidt-return analogues in some systems, citing Hahn (1950) and Waugh, Rhim, and Pines (1972).
claim_evidence.finding: The full-system exact reversal is highly special and not a practical operation for an ordinary gas, but controlled Loschmidt-return/echo phenomena exist in some systems. The article’s revised wording avoids treating practical impossibility as nomological impossibility.
claim_evidence.limitation: The cited experiments are identified in Darrigol’s note but were not independently retrieved or assessed for experimental details; the article does not make a claim about any specific implementation.
claim_evidence.required_edit: The article now calls the reversal extraordinarily fine-tuned and impractical for a macroscopic gas rather than claiming that the reversed state is impossible.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Boltzmann’s response and the interpretation of its probability assumptions remain disputed rather than constituting an uncontested consensus solution.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Introduction §§1.2–1.3 reports divided views on Boltzmann’s work; §3.3 states that Boltzmann’s response varied and is difficult to interpret, and explains criticisms of the immediate reply; §4 details the subsequent approach.
claim_evidence.finding: The source documents interpretive disagreement and limitations; the article now avoids claiming that the probabilistic reply simply resolves Loschmidt’s objection.
claim_evidence.limitation: The account is one scholar’s detailed interpretation; recording its existence does not establish a field-wide consensus or exhaustive review of scholarship.
claim_evidence.required_edit: The article now says the adequacy and historical relation of the replies remain subjects of discussion.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The broken-egg and cosmology questions are editorial teaching prompts, not historical claims attributed to Loschmidt or Boltzmann.
claim_evidence.source_title: Assigned article; checked against cited source scope
claim_evidence.exact_location: Article §6, questions 1–4; source comparison with Callender §§3–3.1, which treats the thermodynamic arrow and Past Hypothesis but does not establish these questions as Loschmidt quotations or historical variants.
claim_evidence.finding: These are educational prompts authored for the entry. Their subject matter overlaps the source, but no attribution to historical authors is made or warranted.
claim_evidence.limitation: This is an editorial classification, not a factual claim made by the cited physics sources.
claim_evidence.required_edit: The revised article labels the questions as teaching prompts rather than claims attributed to Loschmidt or Boltzmann.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The article’s dataset record identifies the matching entry as physics, Loschmidt’s Reversibility Objection, and cites the same SEP page for reversibility, statistical reply, and low-entropy initial conditions.

entries.title: Heisenberg’s Microscope
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the complete article, matching dataset record, and relevant expansion-record entry. Focus: the original gamma-ray microscope setup and assumptions; Heisenberg’s heuristic estimate versus Kennard’s formal state-preparation inequality; measurement disturbance versus state-preparation uncertainty; Heisenberg’s report of Bohr’s critique; and later measurement-disturbance work and experiment. Article prose revised only where necessary for source accuracy. This status records source traceability, not truth of disputed interpretations, consensus, exhaustive literature coverage, or expert approval.
entries.summary: Heisenberg’s relevant 1927 passages, the SEP treatment, and the cited experiment support the revised distinctions between the microscope’s approximate δqδp ∼ h estimate, the Kennard state-preparation inequality, and error–disturbance relations. The article qualifies aperture, recoil direction, Bohr’s reported objection, and the experiment’s scope. Independent review found no material issue.

sources.title: The Physical Content of Quantum Kinematics and Mechanics (translation of Über den anschaulichen Inhalt der quantentheoretischen Kinematik und Mechanik)
sources.author: Werner Heisenberg
sources.publication: Zeitschrift für Physik 43 (1927), 172–198; English translation consulted in a reproduced PDF
sources.access_level: Selected relevant excerpts from a parsed full-text PDF; the PDF was parsed, not merely downloaded, but the entire article was not read cover to cover
sources.exact_locations_read: §1, position/microscope discussion (translation page marked 65; SEP identifies the corresponding original discussion at journal pages 174–175): operational meaning of position, gamma-ray microscope, Compton scattering/recoil, approximate δpδq relation. “Addition in Proof” (translation excerpt page marked 83): Heisenberg reports Bohr’s objection that uncertainty is not exclusively due to discontinuity and that the necessary divergence of the ray bundle leaves the Compton recoil direction spread; the opening and conclusion around this passage were also extracted.
sources.limitations: This is a third-party reproduction of the English translation, not the original German journal copy. Only relevant passages were read. Bohr’s view is directly available here as Heisenberg’s contemporaneous report, not as Bohr’s own 1927 text. The original article’s δp and δq are not given a general standard-deviation definition, and the estimate is semi-quantitative rather than Kennard’s inequality.

sources.title: The Uncertainty Principle
sources.author: Jan Hilgevoord and Jos Uffink
sources.publication: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Spring 2024 edition; Metaphysics Research Lab, Stanford University; originally published 2001, archived edition cited for stability
sources.access_level: Relevant passages in the full HTML entry were read; targeted extracts cover complete pertinent sections and passages, not only the abstract or metadata
sources.exact_locations_read: §2.2, “Heisenberg’s argument”: operational setup, microscope, δpδq ∼ h, and account of Bohr’s Addition in Proof; §2.5, “Mathematical elaboration”: Kennard’s 1927 ΔψPΔψQ ≥ ℏ/2 theorem, standard-deviation definitions, and distinction from Heisenberg’s semi-quantitative account; §4, “The Minimal Interpretation”: state spreads and whether interpretations assign definite values; §6 and §6.1, “The recent debate on error-disturbance relations”: distinction from preparation uncertainty, controversy, and Ozawa / Busch–Lahti–Werner proposals. The expanded §2.2 excerpt also gives the aperture/resolution and photon-direction uncertainty account in Heisenberg’s 1930 lectures.
sources.limitations: A secondary reference work, not a primary source; it interprets the historical texts. Its treatment supports traceability and conceptual distinctions, not a claim that one interpretation is uniquely correct. The archived 2024 page is used as stable citation; the article still links the current SEP entry.

sources.title: Another look through Heisenberg’s microscope
sources.author: Stephen Boughn and Marcel Reginatto
sources.publication: arXiv:1712.08579v1 [quant-ph], 22 December 2017 (preprint version consulted)
sources.access_level: Relevant passages from the full HTML paper were read, including its abstract, introduction, and microscope discussion in §2
sources.exact_locations_read: Abstract; §1 Introduction: historical aim of Heisenberg’s paper, Heisenberg’s use of the microscope, and the authors’ characterization of the argument as heuristic in relation to the state inequality; §2, “Heisenberg’s Microscope and the Indeterminacy Relations”: microscope setup, the δqδp ∼ h estimate, aperture-based reconstruction, and comparison with Kennard’s relation.
sources.limitations: The consulted item is arXiv version 1, a preprint; it is not relied on as the sole authority for any claim. Its broad language about a ‘modern consensus’ is not repeated as a finding here. Its alternative reconstruction and interpretive thesis are not necessary to establish the article’s claims.

sources.title: Experimental violation and reformulation of the Heisenberg's error-disturbance uncertainty relation
sources.author: So-Young Baek, Fumihiro Kaneda, Masanao Ozawa, and Keiichi Edamatsu
sources.publication: Scientific Reports 3, 2221 (2013), published 17 July 2013; DOI: 10.1038/srep02221
sources.access_level: Relevant full-text passages in the PMC-hosted article were read (abstract, introduction, results, and discussion); not metadata or abstract alone
sources.exact_locations_read: Abstract and Introduction: single-photon polarization-qubit test of Ozawa’s relation, noting the tested Heisenberg product relation and scope. Results, “Experimental test of error-disturbance relation,” and Fig. 4 discussion: measured error/disturbance quantities and reported outcome across tested measurement strengths. Discussion: the authors’ qualified conclusion that Ozawa’s relation held while the tested Heisenberg relation failed in this model.
sources.limitations: This is one experiment using a photon-polarization qubit, an indirect/generalized measurement model, and the authors’ operational definitions. It does not test the gamma-ray microscope, refute the Kennard state-preparation inequality, or establish a universal result about all measurement-disturbance formulations.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The thought experiment is attributed to Werner Heisenberg’s 1927 paper; the English title is “The Physical Content of Quantum Kinematics and Mechanics.”
claim_evidence.source_title: The Physical Content of Quantum Kinematics and Mechanics
claim_evidence.exact_location: Title and opening of the translated paper; the paper’s microscope passage in §1. The SEP §2.2 and Boughn–Reginatto §1 identify the 1927 publication and English title. The original German title is Über den anschaulichen Inhalt der quantentheoretischen Kinematik und Mechanik.
claim_evidence.finding: Attribution and year are supported. The article now uses the German title and common English translation rather than treating ‘perceptual content’ as the sole English rendering.
claim_evidence.limitation: The translation of anschaulich varies; the translated paper is a reproduction, and this audit did not inspect the original German printing.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: corrected the metadata to give the German title and the English translation consulted.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Heisenberg considers observing an electron with a microscope illuminated by very short-wavelength, in-principle gamma-ray light to define its position.
claim_evidence.source_title: The Physical Content of Quantum Kinematics and Mechanics
claim_evidence.exact_location: §1, position/microscope discussion, translation page marked 65; SEP §2.2, “Heisenberg’s argument.”
claim_evidence.finding: The primary text explicitly introduces illumination and observation through a microscope, including the possibility of a gamma-ray microscope, to give operational meaning to electron position.
claim_evidence.limitation: The microscope is idealized; the article correctly presents it as a thought experiment, not an existing device.
claim_evidence.required_edit: No separate edit required beyond the revised, source-matched setup description.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Shorter wavelength can improve positional resolution, with the microscope aperture also affecting resolution.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §2.2, discussion of Heisenberg’s original microscope and corrected aperture-based account in Heisenberg’s 1930 lectures; equations (6)–(7) relate resolution and angular aperture.
claim_evidence.finding: Wavelength governs optical resolution, but a wavelength-only account omits the aperture. Article now expressly says aperture matters.
claim_evidence.limitation: The aperture-based formula is from the later, improved presentation in Heisenberg’s 1930 lectures; it should not be imputed verbatim to the 1927 article’s original rough description.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: added that aperture also matters.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Photon scattering transfers momentum to the electron; in the microscope, uncertainty in the scattered photon’s direction produces uncertainty in the electron’s momentum change.
claim_evidence.source_title: The Physical Content of Quantum Kinematics and Mechanics
claim_evidence.exact_location: §1 microscope discussion and “Addition in Proof,” translation pages marked 65 and 83; corroborated by SEP §2.2, which explains Bohr’s point that the recoil change is not precisely determined in the same experiment and the finite-aperture account.
claim_evidence.finding: Scattering recoil is in the 1927 account, but the initial shorthand ‘uncertain kick’ could obscure Bohr’s correction. The passage in the Addition in Proof reports the necessary beam divergence and the spread in recoil direction. Revised article states the angular-range qualification.
claim_evidence.limitation: Bohr’s criticism is available in this source through Heisenberg’s report of it. The simple recoil account is heuristic and depends on the observation geometry and assumptions.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: replaced the generic ‘uncertain kick’ with the finite-angular-range/recoil-direction account and attributed the critique as reported by Heisenberg.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Heisenberg’s microscope argument gives an order-of-magnitude relation δqδp ∼ h, rather than a general fixed measurement-error/disturbance inequality.
claim_evidence.source_title: The Physical Content of Quantum Kinematics and Mechanics
claim_evidence.exact_location: §1 microscope discussion, relation (1), translation page marked 65; SEP §2.2 labels the imprecisions as of order δpδq ∼ h; §2.5 says Heisenberg supplied a qualitative/semi-quantitative formulation without a general definition of δp and δq.
claim_evidence.finding: The paper’s microscope estimate is qualitative/semi-quantitative. The original article’s phrase that the product ‘cannot be made smaller than a fixed quantity’ risked presenting it as a precise inequality and confusing disturbance with general uncertainty.
claim_evidence.limitation: The exact meaning of Heisenberg’s δp and δq is contextual and not standardized as state standard deviations; the estimate is not directly interchangeable with modern error/disturbance definitions.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: replaced the fixed-bound wording with the approximate δqδp ∼ h estimate and stated it is not a general post-measurement bound.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The formal standard-deviation relation ΔxΔp ≥ ℏ/2 is a state-preparation constraint, distinct from the microscope’s measurement-disturbance heuristic.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §2.5, “Mathematical elaboration”: Kennard’s 1927 theorem for normalized state vectors, equation (9), standard-deviation definitions (10), and discussion distinguishing this theorem from Heisenberg’s semi-quantitative relation; §4 and §6.1 distinguish state spreads from disturbance by a measurement.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP identifies Kennard’s 1927 inequality as the mathematically exact standard-deviation relation and explains that it constrains spreads associated with a state; it is not itself a disturbance relation. The article now states this distinction explicitly.
claim_evidence.limitation: The exposition uses the conventional position–momentum notation and ℏ/2 form. The source notes that uncertainty relations can use other spread measures, which are not at issue in the article’s stated inequality.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: added the inequality with its standard-deviation/state-preparation meaning and contrasted it with measurement disturbance.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The microscope is an intuitive/pedagogical illustration, but its disturbance-first picture does not establish that a particle had simultaneously sharp premeasurement position and momentum.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §2.2 on Heisenberg’s operational/epistemological argument; §4, “The Minimal Interpretation,” on state distributions and the fact that interpretations differ regarding definite values.
claim_evidence.finding: The microscope was offered as an intuitive account of the relation, but its disturbance narrative can be read as presupposing a prior momentum value. The formal state relation does not settle the ontology of individual values; the SEP describes interpretations that differ.
claim_evidence.limitation: ‘Pedagogically offers an intuitive illustration’ is editorial framing, not a claim about quantified historical public impact. The source does not establish that the microscope alone made the principle historically accessible to a particular audience.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: removed the broader historical claim that the microscope ‘helped make’ the principle accessible and retained it as explicitly pedagogical framing; qualified the definite-values point.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Measurement disturbance and the spread of outcomes associated with a prepared state are distinct questions.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §4, “The Minimal Interpretation,” defines uncertainty as spreads in outcomes associated with the same state and notes no measurement disturbance is needed; §6 and §6.1 explicitly contrast preparation uncertainty with error–disturbance questions.
claim_evidence.finding: This conceptual distinction is stated directly in the SEP and supports the article’s revised framing.
claim_evidence.limitation: Different authors use varied measures and formulations; the distinction does not imply that state preparation and measurement operations are unrelated in every operational context.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: stated these as distinct questions and avoided presenting them as alternate phrasings of one inequality.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Modern error–disturbance relations formalize the measurement question separately, with results depending on definitions and assumptions.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §6 and §6.1: definition of the measurement-uncertainty question; discussion of the controversy and the Ozawa and Busch–Lahti–Werner proposals; §2.5 on why standard deviations are not the same as measurement inaccuracy.
claim_evidence.finding: The entry describes a separate, controversial literature on error/noise–disturbance inequalities and different proposals. The article’s revised statement avoids implying one universally accepted form.
claim_evidence.limitation: This entry is not an exhaustive literature review; the article does not name or compare every proposed inequality.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: qualified the distinction by noting dependence on definitions and assumptions.

claim_evidence.material_claim: In the 1927 Addition in Proof, Heisenberg reports Bohr’s objection that uncertainty is not attributable solely to the discontinuous recoil; divergence of the ray bundle leaves recoil direction uncertain.
claim_evidence.source_title: The Physical Content of Quantum Kinematics and Mechanics
claim_evidence.exact_location: “Addition in Proof,” translation excerpt page marked 83: Heisenberg acknowledges Bohr’s comments, says uncertainty is not exclusively due to discontinuities, and notes that the necessary divergence of the ray bundle makes the Compton recoil direction uncertain. Corroborating analysis: SEP §2.2, “Heisenberg’s argument.”
claim_evidence.finding: The primary text explicitly reports the point and frames it as Bohr’s criticism. The article now says ‘Heisenberg reports Bohr’s criticism’ rather than implying that the audit consulted Bohr’s separate text.
claim_evidence.limitation: This verifies the contemporaneous report and its substance, not every detail of the private exchange or a complete account of Bohr’s complementarity doctrine. The SEP also notes Bohr’s point that the momentum change’s uncertainty in the same experiment matters.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: named the relevant criticism and clearly attributed it as Heisenberg’s report.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Later experimental work has tested specific error–disturbance relations; the 2013 Baek et al. photon-polarization experiment reported Ozawa’s relation held while the tested Heisenberg product relation failed across the studied measurement strengths.
claim_evidence.source_title: Experimental violation and reformulation of the Heisenberg's error-disturbance uncertainty relation
claim_evidence.exact_location: Abstract; Results, subsection “Experimental test of error-disturbance relation”; Fig. 4 description and Discussion. Full text is available at https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3713528/.
claim_evidence.finding: The article reports an experimental test on a single-photon polarization qubit and concludes, within its specified model and measurement range, that Ozawa’s relation held while the tested Heisenberg error–disturbance product failed. This supports a qualified example, not an unbounded generalization.
claim_evidence.limitation: Specific photonic apparatus, operational definitions, and model; this is not an experiment on the gamma-ray microscope or a test of the Kennard state-preparation inequality. It is one result among multiple measurement-disturbance approaches.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: included the named example and confined the claim to the tested operational model and measurement strengths.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Heisenberg’s microscope is a heuristic, not a rigorous derivation of the formal uncertainty inequality; uncertainty is not simply a consequence of clumsy measurement.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §2.2 characterizes the initial argument and δpδq ∼ h; §2.5 explicitly says Heisenberg gave qualitative examples, no general exact derivation or definition of δq, δp, while Kennard’s theorem is exact; §6.1 distinguishes disturbance relations from preparation relations.
claim_evidence.finding: The qualification already present in the article is warranted and has been strengthened by separating the heuristic and formal relation explicitly.
claim_evidence.limitation: ‘Clumsy measurement’ is informal editorial wording; it should not be read as a technical classification of all measurement error.
claim_evidence.required_edit: No additional edit; the existing caveat was retained and now follows the more precise distinction.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The thought experiment says nothing about consciousness or a conscious mind creating reality.
claim_evidence.source_title: The Physical Content of Quantum Kinematics and Mechanics
claim_evidence.exact_location: §1 microscope discussion describes physical scattering and detection (including photoelectric detection); the relevant passage contains no claim that consciousness causes collapse or creates reality.
claim_evidence.finding: This is a scope-limiting editorial clarification: the cited physical argument concerns an apparatus, scattering, and detection, not consciousness. The consulted passage’s silence does not prove a universal negative about every interpretation of quantum theory.
claim_evidence.limitation: The source cannot establish a comprehensive claim about consciousness in quantum mechanics; the audit only confirms that consciousness is not a premise of this microscope argument.
claim_evidence.required_edit: No edit required; retain as a clearly limited clarification about this thought experiment, not a general conclusion about quantum foundations.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The SEP entry is suitable further reading on the microscope argument and distinction between disturbance and preparation uncertainty.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §2.2 covers the microscope; §2.5 and §4 cover formal state uncertainty; §6–6.1 cover inaccuracy and disturbance.
claim_evidence.finding: The listed further reading directly addresses both the microscope argument and the modern distinction. The article’s live SEP URL and this ledger’s stable archived URL resolve to the same reference work.
claim_evidence.limitation: The SEP is secondary scholarship, not the original 1927 source; article now separately cites the primary translation and one experimental paper in Sources and Attribution.
claim_evidence.required_edit: No change required to the Further Reading entry.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The expansion-record entry and dataset reference support the article’s research provenance as previously recorded.
claim_evidence.source_title: Expansion batch: research record; matching experiments.json record
claim_evidence.exact_location: expansion.md, lines 5–9 and table line 69: on 2026-10-31 the SEP URL was requested and keyword counts recorded; the method explicitly says pages were not read in full and keyword counts do not establish sentence support. experiments.json record id heisenbergs-microscope: reference title/URL/support, date_verified 2026-10-31, article file_path, and summary.
claim_evidence.finding: The single dataset reference matches the article’s SEP reference and the subject. The expansion record was a topic-coverage check only, not passage-level verification; this audit therefore independently read the relevant source passages and consulted the primary text and experiment report.
claim_evidence.limitation: The dataset and expansion record are project records, not independent evidence for the physics. They were not modified. The article now notes that the dataset still lists SEP as its reference.
claim_evidence.required_edit: No dataset change made, as instructed; article provenance was updated to reflect the current source consultation.

Added and distinguished Kennard’s formal ΔxΔp ≥ ℏ/2 standard-deviation/state-preparation relation from measurement disturbance.
Reframed the microscope’s pedagogical role as editorial framing, qualified the interpretation about definite values, and stated the difference between prepared-state spreads and disturbance.
Specified the reported Bohr criticism and attributed it to Heisenberg’s Addition in Proof; added a bounded description of the 2013 Baek et al. experimental result.
Updated Sources and Attribution with the consulted primary translation, SEP entry, and experimental paper, and changed the research check date to 2026-11-01.
Updated the matching dataset publication wording and verification date to match the article.

entries.title: Aristotle’s Sea Battle
entries.reviewer_type: AI-assisted claim-level source audit with independent post-edit review; no human expert review is claimed.
entries.scope: Claim-level audit of article sections 1–10 and associated publication/source claims: scenario and fatalist inference; Aristotle’s response and contested attribution; bivalence, excluded middle, and the summaries of three-valued/truth-gap, branching-time, supervaluationist, Ockhamist, and Peircean approaches; contemporary extensions; editorial framing. Checked against the complete relevant passage of De Interpretatione 9, the cited SEP entry's relevant sections, and a full-text scholarly discussion of interpretive disagreement. This status concerns evidence traceability, not philosophical soundness, consensus, exhaustive literature coverage, or expert review.
entries.summary: The primary chapter, relevant SEP sections, and a scholarly analysis support the article’s account of Aristotle’s fatalist inference, response, and later semantic frameworks. The Ockham passage now specifies that future truth is unknowable to humans but known by God, as SEP §5.1 states. Targeted independent review found no remaining material issue; article and dataset Further Reading URLs match.

sources.title: On Interpretation, chapter 9 (Revised Oxford Translation)
sources.author: Aristotle; translation in The Complete Works of Aristotle, edited by Jonathan Barnes
sources.publication: The Complete Works of Aristotle, vol. 1, Revised Oxford Translation; chapter 9, Bekker 18a28–19b4 (primary text; translation hosted by University of St Andrews)
sources.access_level: Full text of chapter 9 read, including the opening bivalence discussion, fatalist argument, sea-battle example, reply on deliberation and potentiality, and concluding distinction about contradictories.
sources.exact_locations_read: De Interpretatione 9, Bekker 18a28–19b4; especially 18a28–18b16 (past/present contrast and fatalist argument), 18b17–19a22 (necessity, chance, deliberation, and potentiality), 19a23–39 (necessary disjunction but neither outcome necessary; truth-status conclusion). Cross-checked against MIT Classics' E. M. Edghill translation, Part 9, at https://classics.mit.edu/Aristotle/interpretation.1.1.html, including paragraphs from “In the case of that which is or which has taken place” through “not necessary that of an affirmation and a denial one should be true and the other false.”
sources.limitations: Translation evidence establishes what this text says, not which modern interpretation is correct or whether Aristotle's argument succeeds. Translation wording varies; the St Andrews page reproduces the Revised Oxford Translation and is a host rather than the edition publisher. The work is conventionally dated to the fourth century BCE; no precise composition date was checked.

sources.title: Future Contingents
sources.author: Peter Øhrstrøm and Per Hasle
sources.publication: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; first published 2011, substantive revision 11 July 2024
sources.access_level: Relevant full sections read from the complete entry: Aristotle background, formalization of the classical argument, branching-time semantics, Łukasiewicz three-valued semantics, Peircean solution, Prior's Ockhamist solution, supervaluationism, and conclusion/classification.
sources.exact_locations_read: Sections 1 (discussion of Aristotle and the sea-battle, with reference to De Interpretatione 18b23 ff.), 2 (P1–P5 formalization and fatalist inference), 3 (branching time and histories/chronicles), 4.1 (Łukasiewicz), 4.2 (Peircean models), 5.1 (Prior's Ockhamist model and William of Ockham), 5.4 (supervaluationism), and 6 (classification/disagreement).
sources.limitations: Secondary overview, not a substitute for the primary text. It presents a structured taxonomy of positions rather than a consensus survey; classifications and terminology are the authors' chosen framework. It records disagreement but cannot establish that all scholars agree on any one Aristotle interpretation.

sources.title: Is Aristotle’s Response to the Argument for Fatalism in De Interpretatione 9 Successful?
sources.author: M. A. Istvan Jr.
sources.publication: Ideas y Valores, vol. 63, no. 155 (May–August 2014); DOI: 10.15446/ideasyvalores.v63n155.33178
sources.source_type: Scholarly journal article / secondary philosophical analysis
sources.access_level: Full English-language article read from the accessible SciELO full-text page, including the abstract, argument about bivalence/LEM/RCP, quoted Aristotelian passages, interpretation, conclusion, and bibliography.
sources.exact_locations_read: Abstract; sections I–III, especially the discussion of alternative readings at article paragraphs 92–110; passages on De Interpretatione 18a28–33 and 18b27–30 at paragraphs 118–156; and conclusion at paragraphs 260–262. Full text: https://www.scielo.org.co/scielo.php?script=sci_arttext&pid=S0120-00622014000200002
sources.limitations: This is one author's argued interpretation, not a consensus statement. It argues that Aristotle restricts bivalence while retaining excluded middle, and distinguishes this from rival accounts; its claims are used as evidence of a live interpretive position, not adopted as settled fact.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Aristotle's De Interpretatione chapter 9 is the original ancient text associated with the sea-battle puzzle, dated approximately to the fourth century BCE.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Chapter 9, Bekker 18a28–19b4; the SEP entry's section 1 also identifies Aristotle as 384–322 BCE and De Interpretatione IX as the relevant text.
claim_evidence.finding: The primary chapter is the relevant source and explicitly discusses statements about a sea-battle tomorrow. The fourth-century BCE period is consistent with Aristotle's lifetime and is an approximate historical dating, not an exact composition date.
claim_evidence.limitation: The primary passage itself does not date its composition; the period is a conventional historical estimate.
claim_evidence.required_edit: No edit required; retain approximate-period qualification.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The article's setup—today's assertion that a sea-battle will occur tomorrow and its contradictory alternative—is the case Aristotle discusses.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Section 1, paragraph beginning “Central to the discussion…”; quotes both “Tomorrow there will be a sea-battle” and its negation. Primary text: De Interpretatione 9, 18a34–18b4 and 19a23–31.
claim_evidence.finding: The source directly identifies the paired sea-battle propositions and locates the issue in Aristotle's chapter. The article's “someone says today” is explanatory setup, not a quotation or claim that Aristotle gives that exact dialogue.
claim_evidence.limitation: The article is a modern paraphrase; its introductory wording is not presented as a verbatim translation.
claim_evidence.required_edit: No edit required; framing is editorial and is described as a supposition.

claim_evidence.material_claim: If future affirmations and denials must already be true or false, the fatalist inference makes the event or its absence necessary and excludes chance/contingency.
claim_evidence.exact_location: 18a34–18b16: Aristotle sets out the conditional bivalence/necessity reasoning and says it yields that nothing occurs by chance and all is necessary; compare SEP section 2, principles P1–P5 and steps (1)–(8).
claim_evidence.finding: The chapter explicitly lays out the fatalist consequence as a reductio and says a true future assertion cannot fail to happen. The article's concise “if true … cannot fail; if false … cannot occur” summarizes the result, but compresses the premises: the formal classical argument also requires assumptions about past truth/necessity and the future-excluded-middle principle, and not only a bare bivalence principle.
claim_evidence.limitation: The secondary literature disputes the best formal reconstruction of Aristotle's argument; Istvan distinguishes readings based on bivalence, excluded middle, or the rule that one of a contradictory pair must be true and the other false.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Clarified §§3 and 5 to distinguish bivalence from excluded middle and identify the additional assumptions; no change to the basic scenario needed.

claim_evidence.material_claim: On the fatalist inference, deliberation and effort are pointless because a remote prediction would already fix the outcome.
claim_evidence.exact_location: 18b27–19a7, especially the paragraph beginning “So there would be no need to deliberate…”; MIT Edghill translation, Part 9, paragraph beginning “These awkward results…”.
claim_evidence.finding: Aristotle explicitly presents the loss of deliberation and effort as one of the absurd consequences of the fatalist position, including a prediction made ten thousand years earlier.
claim_evidence.limitation: This is the consequence of the position under discussion, not a claim that Aristotle endorses the conclusion.
claim_evidence.required_edit: No edit required; article marks this as what “seems” to follow.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Aristotle replies that deliberation/action can be causative, future possibilities can run in either direction, and the battle-or-no-battle disjunction is necessary without either disjunct being necessary.
claim_evidence.exact_location: 18b17–19a39; especially 18b17–25 on deliberation and potentiality, and 19a23–39 on the necessary disjunction and non-necessity of either outcome. Cross-check: MIT Edghill translation, Part 9, paragraphs beginning “Yet this view leads…” and “Let me illustrate.”
claim_evidence.finding: The text says that deliberation and action are causative, that some future events have possibilities of being and not being, and that it is necessary that a sea-battle either occur or not while neither occurrence nor non-occurrence is necessary. The article's new §3 summary accurately states that distinction.
claim_evidence.limitation: The text's final wording about whether one member is “not already true or false” is itself interpretively difficult; translating that passage does not settle whether Aristotle endorses truth-value gaps.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Added the explicit distinction between the necessary disjunction and non-necessity of either outcome in §3.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Whether bivalence applies to contingent future statements is distinct from whether excluded middle (p or not-p) holds; rejecting bivalence does not automatically require revising all ordinary logic.
claim_evidence.source_title: Is Aristotle’s Response to the Argument for Fatalism in De Interpretatione 9 Successful?
claim_evidence.exact_location: Sections I–II, especially paragraphs 98–110 distinguishing PB (bivalence), LEM (excluded middle), and RCP (one contradictory true, the other false); Aristotle's statement at 19a27 is discussed in paragraph 106.
claim_evidence.finding: Istvan directly distinguishes these principles and argues that Aristotle restricts bivalence but retains LEM; he also describes rival readings. SEP section 2 separately formalizes future excluded middle as P5 and identifies multiple premises. This supports the distinction and shows why the old claim that logic “must be revised” was too blunt.
claim_evidence.limitation: Istvan's proposed interpretation is one contested scholarly argument, not a settled verdict. The entry's revised language presents it as one influential reconstruction rather than the only reading.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Rewrote §3 to distinguish bivalence from excluded middle, add the past-truth/necessity assumptions, and avoid claiming that ordinary logic as a whole must be revised.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Three-valued/truth-value-gap accounts assign future contingents no present true/false value (or an undetermined value), and this is one reading associated with Aristotle rather than an uncontested attribution.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Section 4.1, paragraphs beginning “Łukasiewicz's interpretation…” and “This truth-value, ‘undetermined’…”; section 1 describes the interpretive problems as non-simple. Istvan, section I and paragraph 148, argues for restricting bivalence in Aristotle.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP explicitly attributes a three-valued interpretation of Aristotle to Łukasiewicz and says a contingent sea-battle proposition may be undetermined today. The secondary article argues Aristotle himself restricts bivalence, but also maps rival readings. Thus the article's hedge “often attributed … on one reading” is warranted.
claim_evidence.limitation: This is a disputed historical interpretation; truth-value-gap semantics and assigning a third truth-value are related but not identical formulations, and the sources do not establish a scholarly consensus.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Retained the qualification but clarified in §4 that these are later semantic frameworks, not labels Aristotle himself used.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Branching-time semantics represents multiple possible histories branching from a moment and evaluates future statements against those histories.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Section 3, especially the description of a tree of possible futures, the definition of a model using histories/chronicles, and the explanation that truth values of formulas may vary with the chronicle; see also section 5.1 for branch-relative truth.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP describes branching-time structures as sets of histories/chronicles and distinguishes truth relative to a chronicle from truth settled at a moment. The former article's shared gloss of branching-time and supervaluationist positions as “true or false only relative to how things go” conflated distinct treatments; the revised entry separates them.
claim_evidence.limitation: Branching-time is a family of semantic frameworks, not a single truth-value policy; the source describes multiple competing models.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Replaced the combined, overly broad claim in §4 with a concise separate description of branching-time semantics.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Supervaluationism treats a contingent future statement as neither true nor false at a branching moment when histories disagree, while allowing future excluded middle to be true.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Section 5.4, definition of truth at a moment by supervaluating across every chronicle, the following passage on future contingents lacking truth-values, and the paragraph explaining that P5 is accepted while P3 is rejected.
claim_evidence.finding: This section directly supports the revised description: a proposition is true at a moment only if true on every chronicle and false only if false on every chronicle; a contingent proposition can therefore be neither, while its disjunction with its negation is true. This is not the same as saying the proposition is simply true or false relative to whichever outcome happens.
claim_evidence.limitation: The SEP presents Thomason's account as one modern theory; further debates about the adequacy of supervaluationism are outside this audit.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Separated supervaluationism from branching-time semantics and added its truth-gap / excluded-middle distinction in §4.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Prior's Ockhamist model permits branch-relative future truth without settled truth and rejects the necessity-of-the-past premise; this model should not be conflated with William of Ockham's own doctrine.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Section 5.1, opening definition of Prior's Ockhamist system (accepts P5, rejects P3), the explanation of Ockham(t,c,p) as true at a moment in a chronicle, and the final paragraphs distinguishing Prior's model from William of Ockham's true-future doctrine.
claim_evidence.finding: The SEP directly supports the refined wording. It also shows the original blanket claim “Ockhamist views say the sentence is already true or false” was underspecified: Prior's model assesses plain truth relative to a chronicle, while Ockham's historical position involves a true/false future known by God. The claim that this is simply a truth “not a necessity” was not an adequate description of the semantics.
claim_evidence.limitation: The SEP notes that Prior's system may not fully represent William of Ockham's view; scholarship also uses “Ockhamism” in more than one sense.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Replaced the compressed Ockhamist gloss in §4 with a distinction between Prior's model and William of Ockham's doctrine.

claim_evidence.material_claim: In Prior's Peircean model, genuinely contingent future p and future not-p claims are both false; this is a later semantic position, not Aristotle's stated solution.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Sections 4 and 4.2, particularly the paragraphs after the Peircean valuation clauses: a future statement is true in the Peircean sense only if it holds in all possible futures; if F(x)q is contingent then it and F(x)~q are false, so future excluded middle fails in that model.
claim_evidence.finding: The article's original short account is substantively correct for Prior's Peircean account of genuinely contingent future-tense claims, but it needed attribution and scope: the model defines “will p” with a strong across-histories condition, and the SEP notes that “will not p” is not equivalent to “not will p.” The revised text limits the claim to Prior's model and contingent claims.
claim_evidence.limitation: Natural-language paraphrases may obscure the model's distinction between F(not-p) and not-F(p); do not generalize the result to every proposition expressed with “will.”
claim_evidence.required_edit: Qualified the statement in §4 to name Prior's Peircean model and specify genuinely contingent p / not-p claims.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Scholars disagree about whether Aristotle accepts truth-value gaps or instead preserves bivalence while restricting a related contradictory-pair rule.

entries.summary: Brogaard and Salerno’s SEP treatment supplies the full formal proof, defines knowledge as known by someone at some time, states the epistemic and modal principles, and surveys disputed replies. sources.title: Fitch’s Paradox of Knowability
sources.author: Berit Brogaard and Joe Salerno
sources.publication: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; substantive revision 7 May 2025
sources.access_level: Relevant passages in the full entry were read, including targeted complete sections, not only the abstract or metadata.
sources.exact_locations_read: §1, history and significance; §2, formal knowability paradox, definition of K, proof, and principles A–D; §§3.1–3.5, logical revisions; §§4.1–4.4, semantic restrictions; §§5.1–5.3, syntactic restrictions and objections.
sources.limitations: A secondary reference entry that maps the literature; it does not establish that every verificationist or anti-realist accepts the formal principle, nor does it identify a universally accepted solution.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The unrestricted knowability principle says that every truth is possibly known by someone at some time, and Fitch’s standard conclusion is that every truth is actually known by someone at some time.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §2, equations for KP and the K Paradox; the entry defines K as known by someone at some time and Diamond as possibility.
claim_evidence.finding: The article states the informal principle and conclusion with the temporal/agent scope made explicit.
claim_evidence.limitation: The conclusion follows in the formal system under the associated proof assumptions; it is not a claim about measured human knowledge.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: clarified Kp as someone knowing p at some time and framed the result as conditional on the logic.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The proof assumes an unknown true proposition, applies the knowability principle to the compound proposition that it is true and unknown, and derives a contradiction from the possibility of knowing that conjunction.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §2, NonO, steps (1)–(9): substitution of p ∧ ¬Kp into KP and the reductio showing the conjunction cannot be known.
claim_evidence.finding: The article separates the initial unknown truth from the compound proposition to which the principle is then applied.
claim_evidence.limitation: An informal paraphrase can obscure that the compound—not merely p—is the proposition whose knowability produces the contradiction.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: named the compound and stated that the unrestricted principle applies to it.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The proof uses factivity, knowledge distribution over conjunction in the sketched derivation, classical reductio, necessitation, and modal duality; conjunction distribution is not indispensable to every variant.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §2, principles A–D and lines (4)–(9); §3.1 notes versions that do not require distribution of knowledge over conjunction.
claim_evidence.finding: The revised article identifies the assumptions without implying that conjunction distribution is beyond dispute or needed in every formulation.
claim_evidence.limitation: Different formalizations of knowledge, possibility, time, and admissible proposition substitution can change which assumptions are used.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: explicitly labeled the assumptions of the informal proof and directed readers to the formal derivation.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The proof challenges some verificationist or anti-realist theories but does not refute every view under those labels.
claim_evidence.exact_location: Opening overview and §1: the entry describes arguable anti-realist applications, the historical verificationist reading, and says there is no consensus about whether or where the proof goes wrong.
claim_evidence.finding: The article now ties the consequence to theories that accept unrestricted knowability plus the relevant logic and notes that application to particular theories is disputed.
claim_evidence.limitation: Verifiability, possible knowability, and admissible propositions are not identical across theories.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: narrowed the philosophical consequence and removed any implication that anti-realism as a whole is disproved.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Responses include logical revisions, semantic restrictions, and syntactic restrictions, and these are contested rather than established solutions.
claim_evidence.exact_location: §§3–5: intuitionistic and paraconsistent revisions; situation-based, rigid/non-rigid semantic restrictions; Cartesian and basic-statement syntactic restrictions; §5.3 objections and further Fitch-style challenges.
claim_evidence.finding: The revised summary names the broad families and presents them as proposals with challenges, not settled solutions.
claim_evidence.limitation: A short educational summary cannot reproduce the technical distinctions or all objections in the literature.
claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: distinguished response families and qualified their status.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Fitch published Theorem 5 in 1963 and credited its essential form to an anonymous referee; the SEP reports that the referee was later identified as Alonzo Church, while Fitch’s note records an earlier result attributed by Anderson to W. T. Parry.

claim_evidence.required_edit: Made: clarified the distinct historical attributions and disclosed the limited primary-text access.

edits_made: Rewrote the proof sketch to distinguish the unknown proposition from the compound proposition and to state its main epistemic/modal assumptions.
Qualified the implication for verificationist and anti-realist theories and noted that application to particular theories is disputed.
Summarized the logical, semantic, and syntactic response families without implying that they are settled solutions.

entries.title: The Hole Argument
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the complete article, matching dataset record, and relevant expansion-record entry. Focus: passive coordinate covariance versus active diffeomorphisms; the modern hole construction; the conditional inference to physical indeterminism; Einstein’s chronology and point-coincidence response; philosophical responses; and the scope of extensions to local spacetime theories and gauge freedom. This status records traceability, not that a metaphysical interpretation is true or that the argument settles determinism.
entries.summary: The full relevant portions of Earman and Norton’s 1987 paper support the modern construction and make the physical-indeterminism inference conditional on treating diffeomorphic models as distinct. Norton’s SEP entry supports the active/passive distinction, history, and responses; selected Einstein 1914 and 1916 passages were consulted through Norton’s translation/transcription, not the complete German originals. Stachel’s specialist review provides additional historical context. The article now distinguishes coordinate relabeling from active transformation, avoids implying that relationism follows, and qualifies extensions to other theories. Independent post-edit review is pending.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The modern hole argument involves an active diffeomorphism of the metric and other fields; this is distinct from merely changing coordinate labels.

claim_evidence.exact_location: Introduction pp. 515–517 and §§2–3, especially the Hole Corollary and construction pp. 521–523; SEP §§3 and 7 corroborate the modern formulation.

claim_evidence.material_claim: The mathematical underdetermination implies physical indeterminism only if diffeomorphism-related models count as distinct physical possibilities; accepting Leibniz equivalence removes that inference.
claim_evidence.source_title: What Price Spacetime Substantivalism? The Hole Story

entries.title: Split Brains and the Unity of Consciousness
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the complete article, matching dataset record, and expansion entry. Focus: classic split-brain methods and task-specific findings; limits of inference from everyday behavior; Nagel’s argument about unity and subject-count; current interpretive models; and Pinto et al.’s 2017 detection/localization and cross-hemifield comparison results. This status records source traceability, not settled neuroscience, the truth of a theory of consciousness, expert review, or exhaustive literature coverage.
entries.summary: The classic primary reports support task- and response-dependent dissociations, with patient and testing limits preserved. Nagel’s full 1971 paper supports the philosophical question and his indeterminate-count conclusion, which the article distinguishes from an empirical result. Current SEP and the 2020 review represent the unity debate as open. Pinto et al. support the precise distinction now stated: both patients detected and localized stimuli across the field, while the separate cross-hemifield comparison was tested on Patient DDC alone and was not significantly above chance. The final independent reviewer confirmed that scope; the article and evidence record now specify the exact Pinto sections consulted. No expert review is claimed.

claim_evidence.material_claim: Classic split-brain tests can reveal response- and task-dependent dissociations after commissurotomy, including differences between verbal naming and hand selection for lateralized stimuli.

entries.title: Pereboom’s Four-Case Argument
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the complete article, matching dataset record, and expansion entry. Focus: the four-case progression and like-cases inference; the specified cases and compatibilist-friendly capacities; under-description and disagreement; hard- and soft-line replies; the target of basic-desert responsibility; related manipulation arguments; publication metadata; and accurate disclosure of primary-text access. entries.summary: Full relevant passages in the archived SEP supplement, current SEP entry, Jeppsson’s peer-reviewed analysis, and Caruso’s précis support the article’s narrowed paraphrase of the cases, conditional inference, known disagreement, and basic-desert scope. The article no longer implies that the primary 2001 chapter was read: Google Books lists Chapter 4 but exposes selected image-only pages rather than its argument text; an online excerpt’s provenance remains unverified and is not treated as verified book text. A targeted independent post-edit reviewer passed the revised access disclosure. An earlier reviewer preferred a partial status because the primary chapter was inaccessible; this ledger adopts source_checked for the declared paraphrase/traceability scope because the appropriate full secondary passages were read and the access limit is explicit. No expert review is claimed.

entries.title: Goodman’s New Riddle of Induction (Grue)
entries.scope: Claim-level traceability review of the complete article, matching dataset record, and expansion entry. Focus: Goodman’s definition of grue and its time cutoff; the conflicting future projections; the distinction between instance-confirmation and the projectibility problem; entrenchment; cited naturalness and Bayesian approaches; and the article’s own teaching analogies. This status records source traceability, not that Goodman’s argument succeeds or that one solution is accepted by consensus.
entries.summary: Goodman’s full-text scan supports the grue definition, incompatible post-cutoff predictions, and the entrenchment discussion. The SEP Goodman and Problem of Induction entries contextualize the new riddle and positionality reply. Fitelson’s paper supports a qualified statement that Bayesian analyses depend on measures and assumptions, while the article explicitly marks its priors/model-class takeaway as an editorial inference. Scholz’s 2024 open-access paper supports identifying conceptual spaces as a particular similarity/naturalness proposal and attributing the normative critique to Scholz, not to consensus. The independent final review found no material issue in the declared scope.
